aspect_adaptations: Data-format adaptation: assertions_contracts = schema-as-contract (JSON Schema Draft 2020-12, closed objects, pinned validator as a build-failing gate); bounded_work = document bytes, nesting depth, key/item/string bounds enforced before or during parsing; concurrency = shared-file discipline (one writer, append-only NDJSON, lock+replace) since whole-document replacement does not compose under concurrent writers; memory_ownership = parsed-cost discipline (DOM multiples of wire size, slurp bans, streaming/NDJSON lanes); static_analysis = the pinned validator plus jsonls schema association as the analyzer surface; formatting and determinism carry extra weight here because canonical bytes (jq -S, JCS) are the diff/hash story.

assertions_contracts.best_practice: Matches the current specification state: json-schema.org names 2020-12 as the current version, and under 2020-12 format is an annotation by default that asserts only with the format-assertion vocabulary enabled - exactly the guide's warning. Closed objects (additionalProperties: false) are stricter than the spec default, which is project policy, not a contradiction.
assertions_contracts.evidence: The guide's J2 source is the JSON Schema specification page; Oct 2026 sources confirm 2020-12 remains the latest stable dialect with a successor in development and not released - which the guide itself states.
assertions_contracts.guide_position: Schema is the assertion system: schema written before or with the producer (never fitted to current output), every contract object closed with additionalProperties: false, every field typed and bounded (prefer enum/const over pattern), the draft pinned via $schema to Draft 2020-12, format asserted only when the validator is configured to assert it (annotation by default under 2020-12), and validation as a CI gate with a pinned validator that can fail the build.

bounded_work.best_practice: No JSON RFC prescribes numeric bounds, but RFC 8259 itself warns that implementations may set limits on numbers, strings, and nesting - bounding is the spec-sanctioned posture. The guide correctly separates contract bounds from tool limits: jq 1.8's internal ceilings (parsing depth raised to 10000, arrays/objects capped at 2^29) describe when jq falls over, not what a contract accepts.
bounded_work.evidence: RFC 8259 section 9 (parser limits) is the primary source for the bounds posture; the jq limits figures are the guide's reading of the jq 1.8.0 release notes in its J4 source, and jq 1.8.2 is confirmed as the current release in this pass.
bounded_work.guide_position: Named example bounds per contract - MAX_DOCUMENT_BYTES (1 MiB), MAX_DEPTH (64), MAX_KEYS (256), MAX_ITEMS (10,000), MAX_STRING_BYTES (64 KiB) - enforced before or during parsing where the parser supports it, and a bound exceeded is a rejection with a named error, never a silent truncation.

concurrency.best_practice: No official JSON source defines a concurrent-write model for whole files; the guide's ordering (single writer, then append-only records, then lock+replace, then a database) matches how the ecosystem actually behaves - NDJSON's spec makes each line an independent complete text, which is what makes appends well-defined at all.
concurrency.evidence: The NDJSON specification (the guide's J5) defines the per-line complete-document property the append lane depends on; nothing in RFC 8259 sanctions read-modify-write on shared files.
concurrency.guide_position: Adapted to shared files: whole-document replacement does not compose under concurrency (two read-modify-write writers lose one update silently), so the guide orders the options - one writer per contract file; append-only NDJSON for record streams (single appender, or O_APPEND with line-sized writes and a stated platform assumption); lock + read-validate-modify-replace for the rest; genuinely multi-writer transactional data belongs in a database.

error_handling.best_practice: The exit-status discipline is jq's documented contract and the guide's stated codes are correct; one completeness gap: jq also exits 4 when -e is set and no output was produced at all, a case the guide's list omits (see the final-report defect note - the omission misleads no gate that only distinguishes the codes the guide names, but a gate treating 'no output' as success would want it).
error_handling.evidence: jq-parity references consulted in this pass consistently document the -e family as 1 (last output false/null) and 4 (no output produced) alongside 2/3/5; the guide names 1/2/3/5 only. Flagged as a minor suspected defect in the final report rather than a verdict change, because every code the guide does state is stated correctly.
error_handling.guide_position: Parse errors carry position and are reported against the artifact (never swallowed into a null/empty result); validation errors surface as the validator's structured output (field + constraint), not a collapsed 'invalid'; jq gates use --exit-status (-e) - exit 1 when the last output is false or null, 2 for usage/input errors, 3 for filter compile errors, 5 for runtime errors - and the shell checks the status; failure leaves state unchanged because documents are written only after full validation.

formatting.best_practice: Consistent with the ecosystem's settled tooling: jq is the canonical formatter for stored JSON (its --sort-keys/--indent behavior is stable across the 1.8 line) and jsonls provides the editor surface with schema association; no competing official formatter guidance exists for the format.
formatting.evidence: jq 1.8.2 (2026-06-20) is the latest release per the jqlang project, so the guide's formatter pin names a current tool; the canonical-form rules themselves are the guide's policy and are labeled as such in its Sources.
formatting.guide_position: Deterministic formatter output wins: 2-space indent (jq's default), keys sorted for owned artifacts via jq -S, one trailing newline, UTF-8 without BOM, LF endings, arrays never reordered by formatting; one formatter per repository, pinned - jq for terminal/CI canonicalization with jsonls formatting agreeing in the editor; two formatters in sequence are banned.

memory_ownership.best_practice: Matches documented parser behavior: DOM cost exceeding wire size is the standard property of every mainstream parser the guide's audience uses, and jq's own documentation treats --slurp as whole-input materialization while --stream exists precisely for the bounded lane.
memory_ownership.evidence: The guide's claims are tool-behavior claims sourced to the jq project (J4) and the NDJSON spec (J5); no source consulted contradicts the multiples-of-size cost model.
memory_ownership.guide_position: Adapted as parsed-cost discipline: DOM parsing costs multiples of document size, so section 5's bounds are set from parsed cost, not wire size; jq --slurp over input whose size the caller does not control is forbidden (process value-by-value or with --stream); NDJSON is preferred at design time over --stream at incident time; compiled schemas are built once per process because validation memory counts too.

security.best_practice: The guide's positions are the primary sources' own: RFC 8259 section 4 says names SHOULD be unique and warns behavior with duplicates is unpredictable; I-JSON (RFC 7493) restricts interoperable documents exactly as the guide's profile does; JCS (RFC 8785) is the standards-track answer to hash/signature canonicalization; and jq's 1.8.2 release being largely security fixes (depth limits, NUL handling, hash-seed randomization) is the guide's stated reason for pin currency, with 1.8.2 confirmed current tonight.
security.evidence: RFC 8259 and RFC 8785 were the guide's J1/J3; the jq releases page (J4) confirms 1.8.2 as the current release line the guide names.
security.guide_position: Parser differentials are the core vulnerability: the strictest parser in a chain validates at the boundary and downstream re-parses only bytes the boundary emitted (or the chain standardizes on one parser+version); duplicate keys rejected with a detecting parser where available (jq does not detect them, so jq is never the only boundary gate); __proto__/constructor/prototype forbidden in JS-bound data with safe JS-side merging; JSON embedded in HTML escapes < so </script> cannot terminate the block, plus U+2028/U+2029 awareness; never assemble JSON by string concatenation; schema pattern regexes treated as a DoS surface (anchored, simple, or enum instead); secrets get 0600, no VCS, no fixtures.

static_analysis.best_practice: For a data format the analyzer surface is schema validation plus editor diagnostics, and the guide's pairing (pinned validator in CI, jsonls with committed schema associations in the editor) is how the JSON Schema and VS Code language-server projects document their own usage; the same-server-covers-JSONC point is the language server project's documented capability.
static_analysis.evidence: The guide's J6 (vscode-json-languageserver) documents the json/jsonc capability split it relies on; validator pinning as a contract event follows from the spec's own draft-history (keyword meaning changed between drafts, e.g. items).
static_analysis.guide_position: Adapted to validators: a pinned Draft 2020-12 validator in CI whose failure fails the build; jsonls (vscode-json-language-server, from vscode-langservers-extracted) in the editor with schema associations committed as configuration so editor and CI enforce the same contract; jq as the terminal grammar/gate instrument (jq empty, -e filter gates); a second, different parser as a cheap differential check for wire-lane contracts; validator upgrades treated as contract events because keyword semantics and error output change between versions.

testing.best_practice: Consistent with the RFCs' testable claims (grammar, uniqueness warning, surrogate handling, I-JSON ranges) and with JCS's published test-vector approach to canonicalization; no official source offers a competing test model for documents.
testing.evidence: RFC 8785's vectors are the canonical-form oracle the guide's round-trip tests use; RFC 8259 sections 4/8/9 ground the duplicate, surrogate, and limit fixtures.
testing.guide_position: Half validation, half adversarial: validation covers schema-valid fixtures (including the schema's own documented examples), byte-stable canonical round-trips and JCS test vectors where JCS is used, golden jq filters run with -e verdicts, and NDJSON line-wise processing with the documented empty-line policy; the adversarial corpus runs against every parser/validator in the chain - duplicate keys, precision-loss integer 9007199254740993 and numeric 64-bit IDs, 1e400/NaN/Infinity literals, lone surrogates, one-past-the-bound depth/bytes/items, __proto__ keys, a </script> payload that must emit as \u003c/script, strict-lane rejection of comments/trailing commas/single quotes, BOM and CRLF/unterminated-final-line NDJSON decisions, missing-vs-null-vs-empty fixtures per optional field, and a catastrophic-backtracking pattern probe.

toolchain_pins.best_practice: Every checkable pin is current tonight: jq 1.8.2 is the latest jqlang release (2026-06-20), JSON Schema 2020-12 remains the latest released draft (a successor is in development and unreleased - the guide says exactly this and declines to target it), and jsonls ships in the vscode-langservers-extracted package as the guide states.
toolchain_pins.evidence: The x-cmd/jqlang release data consulted in this pass lists jq-1.8.2 (2026-06-20) as latest with no newer release; Oct 2026 JSON Schema sources describe 2020-12 as the latest stable dialect and the successor (v1/2026) as in development.
toolchain_pins.guide_position: Grammar RFC 8259 restricted to the I-JSON profile (RFC 7493); schema dialect JSON Schema Draft 2020-12 named via $schema, described as the latest released draft with a successor in development that is not a target until it releases and validators support it; terminal toolchain jq pinned on the 1.8.x line (guide names 1.8.2 as current); editor toolchain jsonls (vscode-json-language-server from vscode-langservers-extracted); DAP seat honestly empty.
